title: Why winning half your bets can still lose money
instructions: Read as a knowledgeable, friendly sports analyst explaining a simple idea to an adult beginner. Natural American English, clear and brisk, about 165 words per minute. Warm, conversational, understated. No hype, no shouting, no added words. Keep the same voice and pace throughout. Pronounce devig as dee-vig.

scenes.label: THE HIDDEN COST
scenes.headline:
Win half.
Still lose money.
scenes.detail: When every bet is priced at −110
scenes.narration: Win half your bets and still lose money? At minus one ten, that's exactly what happens. Here's the fee hiding inside the odds.

scenes.label: READ THE PRICE
scenes.headline:
Risk $110.
Win $100.
scenes.narration: Minus one ten means risk a hundred and ten dollars to win a hundred. Win one, lose one: you're down ten dollars.

scenes.label: HOW THE BOOK EARNS
scenes.headline:
$220 in.
$210 paid out.
scenes.narration: Imagine a book takes a hundred and ten dollars on each side of a coin flip. It collects two twenty, pays the winner two ten, and keeps ten. Unbalanced bets can still lose the book money.

scenes.label: THE MARGIN IN THE ODDS
scenes.headline:
52.38%
+ 52.38%
scenes.narration: Those prices each imply fifty-two point three eight percent. Together, that's a hundred and four point seven six percent. The excess is called overround.

scenes.label: REMOVE THE VIG
scenes.headline: 52.38 ÷ 104.76
scenes.narration: To remove the margin proportionally, divide each implied probability by their total. Here, we get fifty percent on each side. That's a market estimate, not proof of the true probability.

scenes.label: USE IT ON FOURTH & VALUE
scenes.headline:
Model.
Market. Price.
scenes.narration: On Fourth and Value, compare our model with the paired fair probability and the consensus at the same line.

scenes.label: THE NUMBER YOU MUST BEAT
scenes.headline: At −110
scenes.detail: Break-even win rate • assuming no pushes
scenes.narration: But at minus one ten, you still need to win more than fifty-two point three eight percent to have positive expected value, assuming no pushes.

scenes.headline:

scenes.narration: De-vig to understand the market. Check the actual price to evaluate the bet. Next: why the same pick can be good at one book and bad at another.
